source_text: Μὴ ὀκνήσῃς ἐκ τοῦ ὀλίγου δοῦναι· μὴ προτιμήσῃς τὸ σὸν συμφέρον ἐκ τοῦ κοινοῦ κινδύνου. Κἂν εἰς ἕνα ἄρτον περιστῇ ἡ τροφὴ, ἐπιστῇ δὲ ταῖς θύραις ὁ ζητῶν, προκόμισον ἐκ τοῦ ταμιείου τὸν ἕνα, καὶ ἐπιθεὶς ταῖς χερσὶ πρὸς οὐρανὸν ἀνατείνας, εἰπὲ λόγον ἐλεεινὸν ὁμοῦ καὶ εὐγνώμονα· Εἷς ἄρτος, ὃν ὁρᾷς, Κύριε, καὶ ὁ κίνδυ νος προφανὴς, ἀλλ' ἐγὼ τὴν σὴν ἐντολὴν ἐμοῦ προ τίθημι, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ὀλίγου δίδωμι τῷ λιμώττοντι ἀδελφῷ· δὸς δὴ καὶ σὺ τῷ κινδυνεύοντι δούλῳ. Οἶδά σου τὴν ἀγαθότητα, θαῤῥῶ καὶ τῇ δυνάμει· οὐχ ὑπερτίθεσαι εἰς χρόνον τὰς χάριτας, ἀλλὰ σκεδαννύεις, ὅταν ἐθέλῃς, τὰς δωρεάς. Κἂν οὕτως εἴπῃς καὶ πράξῃς, ὃν δίδως ἐκ τῆς στενώσεως ἄρτον, σπέρμα γίνεται γεωργίας, πολύχουν ἀπογεννᾷ τὸν καρπὸν, ἀῤῥαβὼν τῆς τροφῆς, ἐλέου πρόξενος. Εἰπὲ καὶ σὺ τῆς χήρας τῆς Σιδωνίας ῥῆμα ἐν τοῖς ὁμοίοις, εὐκαίρως τῆς ἱστορίας μνημόνευσον· Ζῇ Κύριος, ὅτι τοῦτον ἔχω ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ μου μόνον εἰς διατροφὴν ἐμοὶ καὶ τοῖς παιδίοις. Κἂν δῷς ἐκ τοῦ λείπον τος, ἕξεις καὶ σὺ τὸν καμψάκην τοῦ ἐλαίου τῇ χάριτι βρύοντα· τὴν ὑδρίαν τῶν ἀλεύρων ἀκένωτον. Ἐπὶ γὰρ τῶν πιστῶν φιλότιμος ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ χάρις μιμεῖται τὰ φρέατα, τὰ ἀεὶ κενούμενα, καὶ μὴ ἐξαντλούμενα, τὸ διπλοῦν ἀντεισάγουσα. Δάνεισον, ὁ ἄπορος, τῷ πλουσίῳ Θεῷ. Πίστευσον τῷ ἀεὶ εἰς πρόσωπον ἴδιον ὑπὲρ τοῦ θλιβομένου λαμβάνοντι, καὶ οἴκοθεν ἀποδιδόντι τὴν χάριν. Ἀξιόπιστος ἐγγυητὴς, παν ταχοῦ γῆς καὶ θαλάττης ἡπλωμένους ἔχων τοὺς θη σαυρούς. Καὶ πλέων ἐὰν ἀπαιτήσῃς τὸ δάνεισμα, λήψῃ ἐπὶ μέσου πελάγους σὺν τόκοις τὸ κεφάλαιον. Φιλοτιμεῖται γὰρ ἐν ταῖς προσθήκαις. Τὸ τοῦ λιμώττοντος νόσημα, λιμὸς, οἰκτρὸν πά θος ἐστί. Λιμὸς ἀνθρωπίνων συμφορῶν ὑπάρχει τὸ κεφάλαιον, πάντων θανάτων μοχθηρότερον τέλος οὗ τος. Ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ τῶν ἄλλων κινδύνων, ἢ ξίφους ἀκμὴ τὴν τελευτὴν ὀξέως ἐφίστησιν, ἢ πυρὸς ὁρμὴ συντόμως τὸ ζῇν ἀποσβέννυσιν, ἢ θηρία, τοῖς ὀδοῦσι διασπαράξαντα ὅσα καίρια τῶν μελῶν, οὐ συγχωρεῖ τῇ παρολκῇ τῆς ὀδύνης τιμωρηθῆναι. Λιμὸς δὲ ἀργὸν ἔχει τὸ κακὸν, παρέλκουσαν τὴν ἀλγηδόνα, ἐγκαθημένην τὴν νόσον καὶ ἐμφωλεύουσαν, θάνατον ἀεὶ παρόντα, καὶ ἀεὶ βραδύνοντα. Τὸ γὰρ κατὰ φύσιν ὑγρὸν ἐκδαπανᾷ· τὸ θερμὸν καταψύχει· τὸν ὄγκον συστέλλει· τὴν δύναμιν κατ' ὀλίγον ἀπομαραίνει. Ἡ σὰρξ ὡς ἀράχνιον τοῖς ὀστέοις περίκειται. Ὁ χροῦς ἄνθος οὐκ ἔχει. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐρυθρὸν φεύγει, ἐκτηκομένου τοῦ αἵματος· τὸ λευκὸν οὐκ ἔστι, τῇ ἰσχνότητι τῆς ἐπιφανείας μελαινομένης· πελιδνὸν δὲ τὸ σῶμα, ὠχρότητι καὶ τῷ μέλανι ἐλεεινῶς ἐκ τοῦ πάθους κιρνώμενον· γόνατα οὐ βαστάζοντα, ἀλλὰ πρὸς βίαν ἑλκόμενα. Φωνὴ λεπτὴ καὶ ἀδρανής· ὀφθαλμοὶ ἐνασθενοῦντες ταῖς κοιλότησιν, εἰκῆ ταῖς θήκαις ἐναποκείμενοι, ὡς τὰ τοῖς ἐλύτροις ἐμψυγέντα τῶν ἀκροδρύων. Γαστὴρ κενὴ καὶ συμπεπτωκυῖα, καὶ ἄμορφος, οὐκ ὄγκον, οὐ φυσικὴν τῶν σπλάγχνων ἐπίτασιν ἔχουσα, τοῖς ὀστέοις δὲ τοῦ νώτου προσπεπλασμένη. Ὁ οὖν τοιοῦτον σῶμα παρατρέχων πόσων κολάσεων ἄξιος; τίνα δὲ ὠμότητος ὑπερβολὴν κατα λείψει; πῶς δὲ οὐκ ἄξιος τοῖς ἀνημέροις τῶν θηρίων συναριθμεῖσθαι, ὁρᾶσθαι δὲ ἐναγὴς καὶ ἀνδροφόνος; Ὁ γὰρ ἔχων ἐν ἐξουσίᾳ τὴν τοῦ κακοῦ θεραπείαν, ἑκὼν δὲ καὶ πρὸς πλεονεξίαν ὑπερτιθέμενος, εἰκότως ἂν ἐν τῷ ἴσῳ τῶν αὐτοχείρων καταδικάζοιτο.
thought_title: Give from your last loaf and God will repay
orientation: Basil is addressing his congregation directly, urging them to give even from extreme scarcity, and then describes the physical horror of famine to shame those who pass by the starving.
pass_a_gloss: Do not hesitate to give from the little. Do not prefer your own advantage over the common danger. Even if the food is reduced to one loaf, and the one seeking stands at the doors, bring out the one from the storehouse, and placing it on your hands, stretching them toward heaven, say a word pitiful and at the same time grateful: One loaf, which you see, Lord, and the danger is evident, but I set your commandment before my own interest, and from the little I give to the starving brother; give then also to the endangered servant. I know your goodness, I am confident also in your power; you do not postpone favors to a time, but you scatter gifts whenever you wish. And if you speak and act thus, the loaf which you give from the straitened circumstances becomes seed of a harvest, it begets abundant fruit, a pledge of food, a cause of mercy. Say also the word of the widow of Zarephath in similar circumstances, remember the story at the right time: As the Lord lives, I have only this in my house for sustenance for me and the children. And if you give from what is lacking, you too will have the oil jar gushing with grace; the flour jar unfailing. For upon the faithful the grace of God, generous, imitates the wells, the ones always being emptied and not pumped dry, bringing in the double. Lend, you who are without resources, to the rich God. Trust the one who always receives as his own person on behalf of the afflicted, and repays the favor from his own house. A trustworthy guarantor, having his hoarded wealth spread out everywhere on land and sea. And if you demand the loan while sailing, you will receive the principal with interest in the middle of the sea. For he is generous in the additions. The disease of the starving one, famine, is a pitiful suffering. Famine is the sum of human misfortunes, this is an end more wretched than all deaths. For in other dangers, either the edge of a sword brings the end swiftly, or the rush of fire quickly extinguishes life, or wild beasts, tearing with their teeth whatever vital parts of the limbs, do not allow punishment by the prolongation of pain. But famine has the evil idle, the pain prolonged, the disease seated within and lurking, death always present and always delaying. For it consumes the natural moisture; it cools the heat; it contracts the bulk; it withers the strength little by little. The flesh lies around the bones like a spider's web. The skin has no bloom. For the red flees, as the blood is melted away; the white is not there, as the surface darkens with thinness; the body is livid, pitifully mixed with pallor and blackness from the suffering; knees not supporting, but dragged by force. Voice thin and weak; eyes growing weak in their hollows, lying uselessly in their sockets, like the things dried up in the husks of fruits. Belly empty and collapsed and shapeless, having no bulk, no natural tension of the inner organs, but plastered to the bones of the back. The one therefore who passes by such a body, of how many punishments is he worthy? What excess of cruelty will he leave behind? How is he not worthy to be numbered with the savage wild beasts, and to be seen as accursed and a murderer? For the one who has in his power the healing of the evil, but willingly and for greed postpones it, would rightly be condemned in the same rank as murderers.

choices.why: πρόξενος means one who brings about or causes something; 'cause of mercy' captures that the loaf given becomes the agent that procures mercy from God
the phrase means God receives the loan as though it were given to his own face/person, i.e., he takes it personally as done to himself
glossary term for θησαυρός; here it refers to God's stored-up resources spread everywhere
ἀργόν means idle, inactive, not working quickly; famine's evil does not act swiftly but lingers
the eyes lie uselessly stored away in their sockets, like dried fruit in husks
the belly is stuck or molded onto the backbone, conveying the collapse of the abdomen in starvation

bible_refs.note: Ζῇ Κύριος, ὅτι τοῦτον ἔχω ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ μου μόνον εἰς διατροφὴν ἐμοὶ καὶ τοῖς παιδίοις

pass_b_english: Do not hesitate to give from the little you have. Do not put your own advantage ahead of the common danger. Even if your food is reduced to a single loaf, and a beggar stands at your door, bring out that one loaf from the storeroom, place it in your hands, raise them toward heaven, and say a prayer that is both pitiful and gracious: “One loaf, Lord, as you see, and the danger is plain. But I set your commandment before my own need, and from the little I have I give to my starving brother. Give, then, to your servant in danger. I know your goodness; I trust also in your power. You do not postpone your favors to a later time, but you scatter your gifts whenever you will.” If you speak and act in this way, the loaf you give from your straitened circumstances becomes seed for a harvest; it brings forth abundant fruit, a pledge of food, a means of obtaining mercy. Say also the words of the widow of Zarephath in similar circumstances, remembering the story at the right moment: “As the Lord lives, this is all I have in my house for food for myself and my children” (1 Kings 17:12). If you give from what is lacking, you too will have the oil jar overflowing by grace, and the flour jar never empty. For toward the faithful, God’s grace is generous and imitates wells that are always being emptied and never drawn dry, bringing back double in return. Lend, you who are poor, to the rich God. Trust the one who always receives on his own account on behalf of the afflicted, and who repays the favor from his own resources. He is a trustworthy guarantor, with hoarded wealth spread out over every land and sea. Even if you demand repayment while sailing, you will receive the principal with interest in the middle of the ocean. For he is generous in his additions.

The sickness of the starving is famine, a pitiful suffering. Famine is the chief of human disasters; it is an end more wretched than every death. In other dangers, either the edge of a sword brings death swiftly, or the rush of fire quickly extinguishes life, or wild beasts tear apart the vital members with their teeth and do not let their victim be tormented by lingering pain. But famine holds its evil inert, with lingering agony, a disease that sits within and nests there, a death always present and always slowing. It consumes the natural moisture; it chills the heat; it shrinks the body’s bulk; it gradually withers the strength. The flesh lies around the bones like a spider’s web. The skin has no bloom. The redness flees as the blood wastes away; the whiteness is gone, since the surface darkens with leanness. The body is livid, pitifully mixed from the suffering with pallor and blackness. The knees cannot bear weight but are dragged along by force. The voice is thin and weak. The eyes grow feeble in their hollows, lying uselessly in their sockets like acorns dried in their husks. The belly is empty, collapsed, and shapeless, with no bulk, no natural tension of the inward parts, plastered to the bones of the back. The one who passes by such a body—how many punishments does he deserve? What excess of cruelty will he leave undone? How is he not worthy to be numbered among the savage beasts, and to be seen as accursed and a murderer? For the one who has the cure for the evil in his power, but willingly postpones it out of greed, would rightly be condemned on the same terms as those who kill with their own hands.

problems.source_quote: Λιμὸς δὲ ἀργὸν ἔχει τὸ κακόν
problems.why: ἀργόν means 'inactive/unworking', i.e., the evil works slowly, not 'idle' as in lazy

problems.quote: a death always present and always delaying
problems.source_quote: θάνατον ἀεὶ παρόντα, καὶ ἀεὶ βραδύνοντα
problems.why: βραδύνοντα means 'slow/tardy', i.e., death is always coming but never arriving
problems.fix: a death always present and always slow to come

problems.quote: and say a prayer that is both pitiful and grateful
problems.source_quote: εἰπὲ λόγον ἐλεεινὸν ὁμοῦ καὶ εὐγνώμονα
problems.why: εὐγνώμονα means 'fair-minded/reasonable', not 'grateful'; misattributes speaker's tone
problems.fix: say a prayer that is both pitiful and fair-minded
problems.ruling: εὐγνώμονα means 'fair-minded/reasonable', not 'grateful'; misleads reader about the prayer's tone

edits.old: a death always present and always delaying
edits.new: a death always present and always slow to come

edits.old: say a prayer that is both pitiful and grateful
edits.new: say a prayer that is both pitiful and fair-minded

fixed: Changed 'famine has the evil idle' to 'famine holds its evil inert' because ἀργόν means inactive/unworking, not idle as in lazy.
Changed 'a death always present and always delaying' to 'a death always present and always slow to come' because βραδύνοντα means slow/tardy, not delaying.
Changed 'say a prayer that is both pitiful and grateful' to 'say a prayer that is both pitiful and fair-minded' because εὐγνώμονα means fair-minded/reasonable, not grateful.

problems.why: εὐγνώμων means 'gracious,' 'kind,' or 'noble-minded,' not 'fair-minded' which suggests impartiality or justice. The prayer is compassionate and generous-spirited.

πρόξενος means 'one who procures/causes,' but ἐλέου πρόξενος here means the loaf becomes something that procures mercy (from God) for the giver, or a means of obtaining mercy. 'Cause of mercy' is awkward and unclear; 'a means of obtaining mercy' or 'what wins mercy' better captures that the gift secures divine mercy.

problems.quote: as though it were his own person
problems.why: ὑπὲρ τοῦ θλιβομένου means 'on behalf of the afflicted,' not 'as though it were his own person.' The phrase describes God receiving the loan on behalf of the afflicted person, not taking it as his own personal debt. 'As his own person' misrepresents the agency.
problems.fix: who always receives on behalf of the afflicted

problems.quote: do not allow the drawn-out pain to torment
problems.source_quote: οὐ συγχωρεῖ τῇ παρολκῇ τῆς ὀδύνης τιμωρηθῆναι
problems.why: The Greek says beasts do NOT allow the victim to be punished/tormented by the prolongation (παρολκῇ) of pain—i.e., death is quick. The English 'do not allow the drawn-out pain to torment' is garbled: it should be 'do not allow [the victim] to be tormented by prolonged pain' or 'do not permit the torture of lingering agony.' The current English makes 'drawn-out pain' the subject that is not allowed to torment, which is confusing.
problems.fix: and do not let their victim be tormented by lingering pain

problems.quote: a death always present and always slow to come
problems.source_quote: θάνατον ἀεὶ παρόντα, καὶ ἀεὶ βραδύνοντα
problems.why: Source says death is 'always present and always slowing' (βραδύνοντα = slowing/delaying), not 'slow to come'.
problems.fix: a death always present and always slowing
problems.ruling: βραδύνοντα = 'delaying/postponing' (death delays), not 'slow to come' (death is slow).

problems.quote: like the dried kernels of fruit in their husks
problems.source_quote: ὡς τὰ τοῖς ἐλύτροις ἐμψυγέντα τῶν ἀκροδρύων
problems.why: Source says 'like acorns dried in their husks' (ἐλύτροις = husks, ἀκροδρύων = acorns), not 'kernels of fruit'.
problems.fix: like acorns dried in their husks
problems.ruling: ἀκροδρύων specifically = 'acorns', not generic 'fruit'; ἀκρό- = top/height + δρῦς = oak.

problems.quote: Trust the one who always receives on behalf of the afflicted on behalf of the afflicted
problems.source_quote: Πίστευσον τῷ ἀεὶ εἰς πρόσωπον ἴδιον ὑπὲρ τοῦ θλιβομένου λαμβάνοντι
problems.why: Dittography: "on behalf of the afflicted" appears twice, making the sentence unreadable and distorting the syntax.
problems.fix: Trust the one who always receives on his own account on behalf of the afflicted
problems.ruling: 'ὑπὲρ τοῦ θλιβομένου' appears once in source; English duplicates 'on behalf of the afflicted', a clear dittography.

edits.old: Trust the one who always receives on behalf of the afflicted on behalf of the afflicted
edits.new: Trust the one who always receives on his own account on behalf of the afflicted

fixed: Dittography confirmed: the English repeats 'on behalf of the afflicted' twice, which is not in the source. The source reads 'εἰς πρόσωπον ἴδιον ὑπὲρ τοῦ θλιβομένου λαμβάνοντι' — 'receives as his own person on behalf of the afflicted.' The suggested fix 'on his own account' accurately renders 'εἰς πρόσωπον ἴδιον' and removes the duplication.

dismissed.why: πρόξενος means 'cause/producer', not 'means of obtaining'; almsgiving produces mercy from God.
dismissed.note: Here πρόξενος means one who brings something about, so 'a means of obtaining mercy' is a fair rendering.

dismissed.quote: the oil jar overflowing by grace
dismissed.why: βρύοντα means 'gushing/abounding', but 'overflowing' loses the miraculous suddenness; more critically, τῇ χάριτι is instrumental 'by grace' but could be dative of accompaniment.
dismissed.note: 'Overflowing by grace' renders βρύοντα τῇ χάριτι faithfully; the complaint is about style.

dismissed.quote: on his own account on behalf of the afflicted
dismissed.why: εἰς πρόσωπον ἴδιον means 'as his own person/face', i.e., Christ identifies with the afflicted; 'on his own account' obscures the incarnation theology.
dismissed.note: 'Receives on his own account' fairly gives the sense of εἰς πρόσωπον ἴδιον (God counts the gift as given to himself); the proposed 'as his own person' is not English.
